messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: effect coding and more extracetd parametrers for a model
parts:
Balal,
Out of curiosity, I simulated data using the parameters reported and assuming a variance of 1 for the higher order factor.  I then fit the model shown in the diagram, assuming that the above variance was estimated, that the loading of Fluid Reasoning was fixed to 1, and that the unique variance was freely estimated and rounded to 0.  I obtained df = 92.

> Nc <- (16 * 17) / 2
+ ho_var <- 1
+ ho_load <- 4
+ ho_unique <- 5
+ load <- 16
+ cross_load <- 2
+ unique <- 16
+ Np <- ho_var + ho_load + ho_unique + load + cross_load + unique
+ df <- Nc - Np
+ Nc; Np; df
[1] 136
[1] 44
[1] 92
>
 

When I fit the model, the summary returned the above 92 df.  Lavaaan did not provide standard errors, which probably reflects the fact that the scales of the first-order factors have not been fixed.  However, the standardized estimates recovered the parameters within about .01 (with N = 5000) with the exception of the smallest cross-loading (within .04).

Is it possible that the authors reported parameter estimates from an analysis with no fixed scales and no standard errors?

My suggestion would be to follow these three steps:
1. Search the surrounding text for any further clues about how the models were fit.
2. Failing that, check the manual for references to other sources that might explain the analysis in more detail.
3. Failing that, write to the authors and ask for their script, output, or further explanation of the analysis.

Keith

messages.subject: Re: effect coding and more extracetd parametrers for a model
parts:
Balal,
  SAS 9.3 is the current version, which makes the hypothesis of reporting a model without fixed scales implausible.  That kind of thing was more common in the early days of SEM.  The improprieties in the path diagram made me wonder if it was a legacy analysis that had been copied over from edition to edition, but that is not the case if they used SAS 9.3.

  SAS has done a good job of making their docs available online.

https://support.sas.com/documentation/cdl/en/statug/63962/HTML/default/viewer.htm#statug_calis_sect065.htm

  One possibility is that they analyzed a correlation matrix.  However, it is not clear how that might get you to 93 df with 16 observed variables.  If you cannot find more complete reporting, I think you will need to contact the authors.

Keith
